title: Factual infographic: Frost Heave — Ice Lenses That Lift the Ground
tests: General factual infographic; Tuesday scheduled slot 3/6. Direct-canvas orthographic museum information design. Verified mechanism: unfrozen liquid-water migration feeds horizontal segregated ice lenses, which can lift and crack pavement. Visible layers: central cutaway, five-step process, microscopy, lens cross-section, soil comparison, conditions triangle, freeze/heave/thaw sequence, and impact/monitoring band. prompt: Create a finished square museum-quality factual infographic titled FROST HEAVE: ICE LENSES THAT LIFT THE GROUND. The generated canvas itself is the infographic: perfectly front-facing, orthographic, straight-on, edge-to-edge 2D information design, with no visible paper edge, poster, frame, screen, room, desk, tools, hands, cast shadow around the composition, or environmental background. Build eight concrete information layers with crisp museum hierarchy and concise readable labels: 1 central road-and-soil mechanism cutaway; 2 a five-step strip labeled COOLING FRONT DESCENDS, UNFROZEN WATER REMAINS, WATER MIGRATES UPWARD, ICE LENSES THICKEN, GROUND SURFACE RISES; 3 a large microscopy window showing fine soil grains, pore ice, and a connected film of unfrozen liquid water; 4 a clean cross-section of a horizontal segregated ice lens between soil layers; 5 a cautious qualitative comparison of coarse granular soil and frost-susceptible fine soil; 6 a conditions triangle labeled FREEZING, WATER SUPPLY, SUSCEPTIBLE SOIL; 7 a BEFORE FREEZE, DURING HEAVE, THAW comparison showing variable uneven support after melting; 8 a field-impact and observation band showing cracked pavement, a tilted shallow post, a lifted garden stone, subsurface temperature probe, moisture sensor, and layered soil core. Keep the science conservative: frost heave is driven chiefly by liquid-water migration feeding segregated ice lenses, not merely by water expanding where it freezes; frozen soil can contain both ice and unfrozen water; not every wet or frozen soil heaves equally; soil, groundwater, temperature, salinity, loading, and freeze-thaw history affect severity. claims.claim: Frost heave is driven chiefly by liquid-water migration toward a freezing zone and the formation and thickening of segregated ice lenses, not merely by pore water freezing in place.
Frozen soil can contain both frozen and unfrozen water, with the proportions depending on temperature depression, soil specific surface area, and salt content.
Unfrozen liquid water can migrate vertically during freezing and feed the growth of horizontal layers of solid ice called ice lenses.
Ice lenses can separate soil above from soil below and produce large vertical ground displacements called frost heave.
Three conditions govern damaging frost action: freezing conditions, an available water supply, and frost-susceptible soil; not every wet or frozen soil heaves equally.
Soil type and mineralogy, groundwater and flow properties, moisture content, temperature, salinity, and material properties influence freezing behavior and frost-heave severity.
Fine-grained frost-susceptible soils can support more damaging frost action than many coarser soils, but susceptibility depends on the complete soil-water-freezing system rather than texture alone.
Frost heave can lift and damage pavement, producing roughness, displacement, and cracking above the growing ice-lens zone.
Freeze-thaw state in pavement layers can be investigated using subsurface temperature, moisture measurements such as time-domain reflectometry, and coupled heat-moisture models.
During thaw, ice lenses melt and previously heaved ground may lose support or settle unevenly; the exact outcome varies with soil, drainage, loading, and freeze-thaw history.

title: Factual infographic: Coral Fluorescence — Proteins That Shift Light

The generated canvas itself must be the infographic: perfectly front-facing, orthographic, straight-on, edge-to-edge finished 2D artwork with no paper edge, poster, wall chart, placard, frame, screen, desk, room, hands, tools, specimen tray, cast shadow around the composition, or environmental staging outside the designed layout. Show believable tentacles, oral disc, epidermis, gastrodermis containing intracellular dinoflagellate photosymbionts, and underlying skeleton. Place glowing cyan and green host-pigment zones clearly in the oral disc and coenosarc, while keeping the symbionts as separate golden-brown cells in the inner tissue. Build at least nine concrete visual information layers around that central mechanism: 1) the dominant whole-polyp-to-tissue cutaway labeled CORAL HOST TISSUE, ORAL DISC, COENOSARC, PHOTOSYMBIONT CELLS, and SKELETON; 2) a large three-step light-path ribbon labeled ABSORB HIGHER-ENERGY LIGHT → EXCITED PIGMENT → EMIT LOWER-ENERGY LIGHT, using a short blue incident arrow and longer-wave cyan/green emitted arrows without numeric wavelengths; 3) four large macro windows showing CYAN FLUORESCENCE, GREEN FLUORESCENCE, RED FLUORESCENCE, and PURPLE-BLUE CHROMOPROTEIN, with the last explicitly labeled STRONG ABSORPTION, LITTLE OR NO FLUORESCENCE; 4) a protein-scale window showing a simplified barrel-like GFP-family protein around a light-producing chromophore, clearly a conceptual molecular model rather than an atomic claim; 5) a HOST PIGMENT / ALGAL PIGMENT comparison distinguishing colorful host proteins from the golden-brown photosynthetic pigments of symbionts; 6) a shallow-to-mesophotic reef depth strip showing that pigment types and expression vary by species, individual, and environment, without implying one universal depth rule; 7) a LEPTOSERIS CASE STUDY panel showing fluorescent and non-fluorescent colonies co-occurring, with cyan more common in shallower sampled corals, cyan plus green at intermediate sampled depths, and green more common in deeper sampled corals; 8) a POSSIBLE LIGHT-FIELD EFFECTS panel showing two cautious branches, PHOTOPROTECTION and LIGHT ENHANCEMENT, both headed PROPOSED AND CONTEXT-DEPENDENT; 9) a WHAT THE CASE STUDY FOUND comparison showing similar measured symbiont abundance, pigments, photosynthetic performance, and excitation spectra in fluorescent versus non-fluorescent Leptoseris, ending with the concise conclusion NO SIGNIFICANT PHOTOSYNTHESIS ENHANCEMENT FOUND IN THIS STUDY; 10) a compact uncertainty band reading BIOLOGICAL ROLES VARY — PRECISE FUNCTIONS ARE NOT FULLY RESOLVED.

Use a bold radial information architecture unlike recent weather, biomechanics, and insect-anatomy graphics: central coral cutaway in the lower-middle; light-path ribbon arcing across the upper third; four oversized pigment macro windows forming a left-side color ladder; Leptoseris depth transect as a tall right-side column; host-versus-symbiont and case-study comparisons as two broad lower bands. sources.title: Fluorescent proteins in dominant mesophotic reef-building corals
The role of host pigments in coral photobiology

claims.claim: Many coral host pigments are green-fluorescent-protein-like pigments, and fluorescent forms span cyan, green, and red emission colors.
A fluorescent protein absorbs higher-energy light and emits lower-energy light at a longer wavelength.
Non-fluorescent chromoproteins can absorb visible light strongly while producing little or no fluorescence, and commonly contribute purple-blue coloration.
The pigment types and their expression can differ among coral species and among individuals of the same species.

Coral host pigments can alter the local light field inside coral tissue; proposed photobiological effects include photoprotection or light enhancement depending on species and environment, but their precise biological roles are not fully resolved.

In four Hawaiian mesophotic Leptoseris species studied at 65-125 m, cyan and green fluorescence was localized mainly in the coenosarc and/or oral disc, and fluorescent and non-fluorescent colonies co-occurred across the investigated depths.
In that Leptoseris study, cyan fluorescent protein was more common at shallower sampled depths, green fluorescent protein at deeper sampled depths, and both occurred at intermediate sampled depths.

The Leptoseris study found similar symbiont genotypes, abundance, pigments, photosynthetic efficiency, photosynthetic rates, and chlorophyll excitation spectra in fluorescent and non-fluorescent corals, so those fluorescent proteins were unlikely to significantly enhance symbiont photosynthesis in the studied corals.

Coral tissue can contain intracellular dinoflagellate photosymbionts in the endodermis, while host fluorescent pigments occupy species-dependent tissue locations and modify the light microenvironment around them.

title: Factual infographic: Colobopsis explodens — The Ant That Ruptures to Defend

Volatiles from the Mandibular Gland Reservoir Content of Colobopsis explodens Worker Ants

claims.claim: Colobopsis explodens is a real ant species in the Southeast Asian Colobopsis cylindrica species group and was described from material associated with Borneo, Thailand, and Malaysia.
Field observations of Colobopsis explodens were made in lowland dipterocarp rainforest in Brunei, where colonies occupied trees and wooden nest cavities.
Minor workers are reddish-brown, measure about 4-7 mm, and carry enlarged mandibular-gland reservoirs extending through much of the body.
During close territorial conflict, a minor worker can rupture the integument of its gaster, an irreversible self-sacrificial behavior called autothysis.
Autothysis releases bright yellow, sticky mandibular-gland reservoir contents onto an arthropod opponent, helping restrain, repel, or kill the opponent.
The defensive sequence is a close-contact mechanism, not a fireball or pressure explosion: the gaster ruptures and transfers adhesive secretion to the opponent.
Major workers have enlarged plug-shaped heads and can block entrances to wooden nests, a defensive behavior known as phragmosis.
Chemical analyses found a complex mixture of volatile compounds in the minor workers' mandibular-gland reservoir contents, including alkanes, carboxylic acids, and phenolic compounds.

Researchers proposed that likely irritant and antibiotic phenolic constituents may contribute to defense against arthropod opponents or microbes, but the functions of many individual compounds remain unresolved.
The self-sacrificial rupture behavior belongs to minor workers and should not be implied to occur in every caste or every encounter.
